title: The largest single cases, as their documents describe them
question: Which construction contracts grew by the most dollars, and how does each document describe the growth?
finding: The Controller's close-out memorandum on the Public Utilities Commission's Crystal Springs/San Andreas contract with Kiewit Infrastructure West Company records an original amount of $99.8 million and a final amount of $132.4 million after modifications and change orders, +33%. The Central Subway's main contract with Tutor Perini Corporation was awarded at $839.7 million and stood at $1.20 billion at Modification No. 147; the 146 amendments before it are described in the item as "a 38 percent increase". The largest construction-manager contract, Southeast Water Pollution Control Plant Biosolids Digester Facilities Project (Biosolids Project) with MWH Constructors/Webcor Builders Joint Venture, is one that the Commission amended to add work and price: $938.8 million before the first amendment on file and $2.25 billion after the latest. At the Airport, 35 design-build contracts are enlarged by serial "Phase" approvals rather than modifications; the largest, with Turner Construction Company for Terminal 3 West, went from $152.5 million at its first phase on file (2019-02-19) to $2.06 billion at phase 21 (2026-08-25). A phase approval funds the next part of a job whose full size was known; it is not a change order.
how: The commissions that oversee construction (Public Utilities, Airport, Port, Public Works since late 2022, and the transit Board) vote on contract changes above what staff may approve, and on close-outs; those items were read into one record per contract number and department. The first figure is the original amount where an item prints it (or, for the Public Utilities Commission, the award in its minutes); otherwise it is the amount that stood before the first change on file, which already includes earlier staff-approved changes and so understates growth. The latest figure is the final amount at close-out, or the total in the latest item. Where the Board of Supervisors approved the same change as a commission, the commission's row is kept and the Board's dropped; where a numbered modification appears twice, the later row is kept. Design-build and construction-manager contracts, which grow as phases and work packages are added, and professional-services contracts are kept apart from fixed-price construction. Listed: the close-out the Controller reviewed; the twelve fixed-price construction contracts that rose by the most dollars over their first figure; the six construction-manager or design-build contracts that did; and the eight Airport design-build contracts with the largest capacity, which grow by phase approvals. "As printed" is the first 25 words of the latest item for the contract.
limits: Amounts and days are copied from agenda items and minutes and parsed from their wording; contractor names are phrases from the item text. A total in an item is an authorization, often including contingency, not money paid. Most Public Works rows are agenda items as proposed, because minutes before 2025 are not posted. A contract appears in these files only when a change needed a commission vote, so small changes approved by staff are invisible, and departments set that line differently: rates can be compared within a department, not across. Change orders for conditions found underground and for work the owner adds are an ordinary part of construction. The kinds are not alike. A fixed-price contract that rises did so through change orders and claims. A construction-manager or design-build contract is signed for early work and enlarged as later packages are priced, so its first figure was never meant to be the whole price. Airport phases are the same thing by another name. Only the first kind is growth in the ordinary sense, and even there several items say the City added the work.
